findings.quote: **Short stories** and **novel excerpts** can be studied through plot
findings.problem: The lesson's title term is set in bold as if defined, but the lesson never says what an excerpt is: a part taken from a longer work. The word returns in the heading of Example 10. Compared with base 7032eec5, the rewrite also cut the base's excerpt teaching (Example 4 and the strategy line that an excerpt can prepare an event without guaranteeing its outcome), so nothing states why reading only a part limits what a reader can claim. Example 10 step 3 keeps the reasoning in one case but does not supply the meaning. The audit goal names excerpt inferences. The lesson is at 1,698 of 1,700 words.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness; writer rules, rules added after round 1, rules 1 and 3; brief, audit Goal; base revision 7032eec5

findings.quote: A flat character can change, and a round character can stay the same.
findings.problem: This case is stated but never worked. Example 5 classifies only a round dynamic character (Dino) and a flat static one (Mrs. Reyes), the two pairs that fit the false equation Trap 1 warns about. No example shows a character whose two answers do not line up that way. The brief lists this item as: examples none, with possible combinations stated without separate demonstrated cases, at curriculum class through upcat-L095.
findings.source: Checklist L18; lead ruling 1; brief item Distinguish complexity from change, ref upcat-L095 (curriculum)

findings.quote: **Plot** is the order in which a story tells its events.
findings.problem: This paragraph has four sentences; the limit is one to three short sentences. This is the round 1 L22a finding, still open for this paragraph.
